title: Lantern Marsh
kicker: GENERATIVE SYSTEMS · AMBIENT 4: ON LAND (1982) · A LANDSCAPE YOU WALK THROUGH
idea: Ambient 4: On Land (1982) is music made partly from non-instruments (chains, sticks, stones) and from old tapes reworked into new music, which its sleeve notes compare to composting. The sounds live their own lives at a distance, some beyond hearing, so the listener stands inside a landscape where foreground and background are no longer separate. Lantern Marsh is a map you walk across. Eight sources (your sounds, or built-in chain, sticks, stones, rooks, frogs, insects, a drone and a far bell) each keep their own irregular time. Where you stand decides what you hear: distance sets level, darkness, width and reverb. COMPOST turns the last few seconds of the landscape into a slow bed of new sound.
controls: 8 source slots plus a compost slot; drag sources and the listener on the map; per source on/off and its own period; earshot radius, distance darkness, distance reverb, foreground/background flatten; tape speed and wow (time distortion); sources wander and the listener walks; compost: capture the landscape and replay it as slow grains, auto compost; ten place presets named after On Land tracks.
how: Press PLAY and listen. Drag the small standing figure (the listener) across the marsh: nearby sounds become loud, bright and dry, far ones dark, wide and wet, and some go out of earshot. Drag the white objects to move sources. C composts the last eight seconds into the compost slot, which then breaks down slowly underneath. W lets the sources wander, K makes you walk, T halves tape speed, F flattens foreground and background. Load your own field recordings into the eight slots with the deck (D).
try: Record ten short sounds in one real place you know (a gate, a dog, a kettle, a far road, keys, a bird) and load them as a folder. Lay them out on the map roughly where they were, then walk the listener slowly from one end to the other and record a WAV of the walk.

Load old loops or abandoned bounces of your own into the slots, play for a minute, then press C a few times. Mute the original sources and keep only the compost: that is On Land's composting, turning what would be waste into nourishment.

Drag one source far beyond the earshot ring so you cannot hear it, then switch WANDER on. It keeps living its own life out there and now and then drifts close enough to hear. Turn FLATTEN up and down and listen for when foreground and background stop being separate.

manifesto.name: Ambient 4: On Land (sleeve notes)
manifesto.author: Brian Eno
manifesto.where: Sleeve notes to Ambient 4: On Land (E.G. Records, 1982), reprinted in later editions
ideas: On Land is music about places, some real and some half-remembered. Eno says he knew Lantern Marsh, near Dunwich in East Anglia, only from a map and from imagining it.
He used non-instruments such as chains, sticks and stones, and recordings of frogs, insects and rooks, alongside synthesisers and bass.
He reused and reprocessed old recordings, which he compared to composting: turning waste into nourishment.
He wanted much of the sound at a considerable distance from the listener, some of it out of earshot, and wanted sounds to live their own lives separately from one another.
In a landscape like this, everything is part of it: there is no longer a sharp distinction between foreground and background.
He said the record was inspired by Fellini's film Amarcord and by Teo Macero's production of Miles Davis's 'He Loved Him Madly'.
In our words: Eno used non-instruments: chains, sticks and stones.
In our words: He compared reusing old recordings to composting: turning waste into food.
In our words: In a landscape like this, foreground and background stop being separate.
manifesto.system: Every source is a point on a map with its own period and irregularity, so nothing shares a beat: hits come in small clusters at uneven times, and the insects and drone are long, overlapping loops. Each source has its own channel: level falls with the square of distance, a lowpass darkens it (air absorbs high frequencies), the pan follows its direction from you, and the reverb send grows with distance. Beyond the earshot ring a source is silent but keeps its schedule. FLATTEN brings everything to one level while keeping the darkness and wetness of distance. TAPE slows every playback (pitch and time together) and WOW wobbles it, as with old tape. COMPOST grabs the last eight seconds of the master, places it in slot 9 and plays it back as slow, dark grains.
manifesto.dubious: The ten places are this tool's own impressions of the track titles, not reconstructions of the recordings.

title: In C, Your Way
kicker: MINIMALISM · IN C (1964) · A PULSE, 53 CELLS, ANY NUMBER OF PLAYERS
idea: In C (1964, premiered at the San Francisco Tape Music Center in November 1964) gives a group of any size 53 short melodic patterns and a few rules. Each player works through the patterns in order and repeats each one as many times as they like, so the parts slide against each other, and a steady pulse of eighth notes on high C holds everything together. The rules matter more than the notes: don't hurry, stay within two or three patterns of each other, drop out and listen, and meet in unison at least once or twice. This instrument puts those rules on sliders for up to twelve players, using your sounds. Its 53 cells are its own, written to follow the broad harmonic path of the piece (C, then a turn towards G with F sharp, then B flat near the end). You can edit any cell or write a new set from a seed.
controls: 8 slots (pulse plus seven player timbres, all tuned to C4); players 2 to 12; how long each player stays on a cell (min and max repeats); how far apart players may drift (spread); drop-out chance; rhythmic shifts; augmentation; octave spread; dynamics; pulse level and on/off; a seed that writes a new set of 53 cells; a cell editor; unison, ending and restart.
how: Press PLAY. The pulse starts and players enter one by one, each repeating cell 1 before moving on. Watch the strip of 53 cells: dots are players, and nobody runs more than SPREAD cells ahead. U brings everyone into unison on the leading cell, E starts the ending (everyone moves to 53, swells, then drops out), N writes a new set of cells. Load your own one-shots tuned near C into slots 2 to 8 with the deck (D) and every player plays your sounds.
try: Load eight short tonal one-shots from Splice (a pluck, a mallet, a bell, a sung 'ah', a muted guitar) roughly in C, one per slot. Set PLAYERS to 12 and SPREAD to 2 and let it run through all 53 cells. Record the whole run as a WAV: it will last about as long as your stay settings allow.

Put a percussive sound you recorded yourself (a tapped glass, a key on a radiator) in slot 1 as the pulse, set PULSE level high, and use only three players with long stays (min 8). Listen for the moment the three parts lock into a new composite rhythm that nobody is playing on their own.

Write your own cells: select cell 1, type a short figure of your own in the editor (for example 0:1 4:1 7:2), and do the same for a few more. Then turn SHIFT and AUGMENT up so players move your figures off the beat and double their lengths.

manifesto.name: In C (1964), with its performing directions
manifesto.author: Terry Riley
manifesto.where: First performed on 4 November 1964 at the San Francisco Tape Music Center; first recording on Columbia Masterworks (1968). The performing directions are printed with the score.
ideas: 53 short patterns, played in order by any number of musicians, each player repeating each pattern as often as they choose before moving on.
A steady eighth-note pulse on the top Cs of a piano or a mallet instrument; Steve Reich, who played at the premiere, suggested the pulse.
Do not hurry: stay on a pattern long enough to interlock with the patterns others are playing.
Stay within two or three patterns of each other; listen, and drop out from time to time.
Patterns can be started at any time, shifted against the pulse and played at different octaves; the group should aim to come together in unison at least once or twice.
The ending: when everyone reaches the last pattern, the group swells and fades, dropping out one by one.
In our words: Don't rush from pattern to pattern; stay on each one long enough to lock in with what others are playing.
In our words: Players should stay within two or three patterns of each other.
In our words: The group should try to come together in unison once or twice.
manifesto.system: The pulse plays eighth notes on high C from slot 1. Each player has a timbre (slots 2 to 8 in turn), an octave, a stereo place, and a current cell. A player repeats its cell a random number of times between STAY MIN and STAY MAX, then moves on, but only if it would stay within SPREAD cells of the player furthest behind; otherwise it keeps repeating, as the directions ask. At each repeat a player may drop out to listen (DROP OUT), insert a short rest so its pattern shifts against the pulse (SHIFT), or double its note lengths (AUGMENT). Each player swells and fades on its own slow curve. UNISON moves everyone to the leading cell on the same beat. ENDING sends everyone to cell 53, builds, then players stop one by one and the pulse ends last.
manifesto.dubious: The 53 cells here are generated by this tool and are not Terry Riley's patterns; they borrow only the broad harmonic path of In C. For the real piece, use the published score.

title: Zeno's Race
kicker: ZENO OF ELEA (c. 450 BC) · FOUR PARADOXES OF MOTION, AS TIME IN MUSIC
idea: Zeno of Elea argued that motion is impossible. Before you reach a goal you must first reach the half-way point, then half of what is left, forever. Swift Achilles can never catch the tortoise, because he must first reach the place the tortoise has just left. A flying arrow, at any instant, is simply where it is, so it is at rest. And in the stadium, a body seems to pass something in half the time it takes to pass something else. We know these arguments mainly through Aristotle's Physics, which also answers them: time, like distance, can be divided without end, and infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite time. This instrument turns each paradox into a musical process. The Z switch flips between Zeno's view (steps that never arrive, an arrow frozen at every moment) and Aristotle's (the steps add up, the riser lands, Achilles overtakes).
controls: 8 slots (half-way voice, goal hit, tortoise, Achilles, arrow texture, three stadium rows); ZENO or ARISTOTLE view (Z); level for each paradox; dichotomy race length and target interval; Achilles' speed ratio, the tortoise's head start, melody scale and root; arrow moment size, hold, flight speed; stadium speed and frame of reference (still row or moving row); drone.
how: Press PLAY. You hear the four paradoxes at once: a half-way riser, a slow melody (the tortoise) chased by a fast copy of itself (Achilles), a granular arrow, and three rows of drums sliding past each other. Press Z to switch between Zeno and Aristotle. In Zeno's view the riser keeps halving and never lands; in Aristotle's it accelerates, lands and drops. Keys 1 to 4 solo a paradox, 5 plays all of them. F switches the stadium's frame of reference. Put your own sounds in the deck (D): a vocal or texture in slot 5 makes the arrow most audible.
try: Load a long vocal or field recording into slot 5 (the arrow). Solo the arrow (3), set MOMENT to 0.08 s and HOLD to 6, and flip Z back and forth: the same sound in frozen stills or in continuous flight. Record each and compare.

Put one of your own melodic loops' single notes (a pluck or keys sample in C) into slots 3 and 4. Solo Achilles (2), set SPEED to 1.5 and HEAD START to 8, and listen in Aristotle's view: the canon gets tighter until he passes. Then switch to Zeno's view: every stage gets a whole bar, so the canon tightens and slows until it freezes, and he never passes.

Load three of your drum one-shots into slots 6, 7 and 8. Solo the stadium (4) at speed 1 and press F: the same three patterns, heard first from the still row and then from the row that moves. Notice the third row now seems to move twice as fast.

manifesto.name: The paradoxes of motion
manifesto.author: Zeno of Elea (c. 490 to c. 430 BC), as reported and answered by Aristotle
manifesto.year: c. 450 BC (Zeno); Aristotle's Physics, 4th century BC
manifesto.where: Aristotle, Physics, Book VI, chapter 9 (translation by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye)
ideas: The Dichotomy: to reach a goal you must first reach the half-way point, then half the remainder, and so on without end.
Achilles and the tortoise: the pursuer must first reach the place the pursued has left, by which time the pursued has moved on, so the slower one always keeps a lead.
The Arrow: at any single instant a flying arrow occupies a space equal to itself, so at every instant it is at rest, and therefore it never moves.
The Stadium: rows of equal bodies passing each other in opposite directions seem to show that half a time equals double that time.
Aristotle's answer: time is not made of indivisible moments. Time and distance are both endlessly divisible, so endlessly many smaller and smaller steps can be completed in a finite time.
quotes: whatever moves must reach the halfway point before it reaches the end
Aristotle, Physics VI.9, reporting Zeno (public domain; our translation from the Greek)
the fastest runner never catches the slowest, because the pursuer must first reach the place the pursued has just left, so the slower one always stays ahead
Aristotle, Physics VI.9, reporting Zeno (public domain; our translation)
the flying arrow is at rest
Aristotle, Physics VI.9, reporting Zeno (public domain; our translation)
time is not made up of indivisible nows
Aristotle, Physics VI.9 (public domain; our translation)
manifesto.system: DICHOTOMY: a race of RACE bars towards a goal pitch (TARGET semitones up). In Zeno's view each step lasts one beat, but each covers half of what is left in pitch and brightness, so the line gets endlessly close and never lands. In Aristotle's view each step also takes half the time of the last, so the steps add up to exactly the race length (1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 ... = 1): the roll accelerates, lands on the goal hit and starts again. ACHILLES: a 16-note melody played at walking pace by the tortoise, starting HEAD START notes ahead, and the same melody chased SPEED times faster by Achilles. In Aristotle's view he simply runs and overtakes; in Zeno's view each stage (reaching where the tortoise just was) is given one whole bar. The gap shrinks by the speed ratio at every stage, so both runners seem to slow down: the canon tightens and freezes, he never passes, and the race starts again. ARROW: grains of slot 5 one MOMENT long. Zeno: each grain is repeated HOLD times at the same place, a still for every moment. Aristotle: the place moves continuously. STADIUM: three rows of hits on a 16-step grid; the first stands still, the second moves right and the third moves left, one step per bar times SPEED. FRAME hears them from the moving second row instead, so the first row moves one way and the third moves twice as fast.
manifesto.dubious: Zeno's own book is lost; the paradoxes survive in later reports, mainly Aristotle's, so their exact original wording is unknown.

title: Make Way for Magic
kicker: REFUS GLOBAL · MONTREAL, 9 AUGUST 1948 · PAINT WITHOUT INTENTION, AND HEAR IT
idea: Refus global (Total Refusal) was published in Montreal on 9 August 1948 by the painter Paul-Émile Borduas and fifteen other Automatistes, among them Jean-Paul Riopelle, Marcelle Ferron, Françoise Sullivan, Fernand Leduc and Claude Gauvreau. Four hundred copies were printed. It rejected the closed, fearful society of Duplessis-era Quebec and called for art made by automatism: gestures that come before conscious intention. Its most famous lines are a list of what to make way for: magic, objective mysteries, love and necessity. Here you paint gestures and the gestures play. Left to right is time, height is pitch and the speed of your hand is how loud and bright it is. There are four layers, one for each 'Place à', four brushes (Riopelle-like dabs, lines, splashes and Gauvreau-like syllables), an automatic hand that paints by itself, REFUS to wipe everything and RESPONSABILITÉ to keep what you choose.
controls: 8 slots (magic, objective mysteries, love, necessity, syllables voice, splash texture, ground, refusal crash); paint with four brushes on four layers; loop length; scale, root and pitch range; automatic hand (rate and wildness); strokes fade unless kept; REFUS wipes, RESPONSABILITÉ keeps, undo; play-as-you-paint; ground level; Gemini paints strokes from a sentence (optional, your own key).
how: Press PLAY: a painting made by the automatic hand is already playing. Draw on the page with the mouse or a pen. Fast strokes are loud and bright, slow strokes soft and dark; high is high. 1 to 4 choose the layer (magic, mysteries, love, necessity), Q W E T choose the brush (dab, line, splash, syllables). A turns the automatic hand on and off. X is REFUS: wipe everything. K is RESPONSABILITÉ: keep every stroke now on the page so it no longer fades. Backspace undoes. Load your own sounds per layer in the deck (D).
try: Load four of your own one-shots (something bright, something strange, something warm, something hit) into slots 1 to 4. Close your eyes, or look away from the screen, and paint for thirty seconds without deciding anything. Then listen and press K only on what you want to keep.

Record yourself speaking nonsense syllables for twenty seconds, in the spirit of Claude Gauvreau's invented sound poems, and load it into slot 5. Choose the SYLLABLES brush (T) and draw long, fast, falling strokes: each stroke cuts new syllables out of your voice.

Turn the automatic hand on (A), set WILDNESS high and FADE to 2 loops, and let the page paint, play and forget itself while you record a WAV. Press X once, in the middle, for a total refusal, and listen to what grows back.

manifesto.name: Refus global
manifesto.author: Paul-Émile Borduas and fifteen co-signatories (the Automatistes), including Jean-Paul Riopelle, Claude Gauvreau, Marcelle Ferron, Fernand Leduc and Françoise Sullivan
manifesto.where: Published in Montreal on 9 August 1948 in an edition of 400 copies, with a cover by Jean-Paul Riopelle
ideas: A total refusal of the fear, conformity and religious control that, the signatories said, held Quebec society back.
Automatism: making work through spontaneous gesture, before conscious intention or reason can take over, opening the way to the unconscious.
A rallying list of what to make room for: magic, objective mysteries, love and necessity.
Refusal is joined to full responsibility: the artists accept the consequences of their freedom.
Borduas lost his teaching post as a result of the manifesto, and the text is now seen as a starting point of Quebec's Quiet Revolution.
In our words: The manifesto ends by making room for magic, for objective mysteries, for love and for necessity.
In our words: It refuses all intention, which it calls reason's harmful weapon.
In our words: Against total refusal it sets full responsibility.
manifesto.system: Every stroke you paint is kept as a list of points with their times. When a stroke ends it is turned into events: a DAB makes a hit every few pixels, a LINE makes a gliding chain of grains that follows the height of the stroke, a SPLASH scatters grains of the splash texture and the layer sound around each point, and SYLLABLES cut short pieces from the voice slot. Horizontal position is the moment in the loop, vertical position is a degree of the chosen scale, and the speed of the hand sets level and brightness. Each layer has its own sound slot. Strokes fade a little on every loop and vanish after FADE loops unless RESPONSABILITÉ has kept them. The automatic hand draws random-walk strokes with its own speed and wildness, so painting without intention is built in.
manifesto.dubious: This is a musical reading of the manifesto; the Automatistes painted and wrote, and the mapping from gesture to sound is this tool's own.

title: Pavement Garage
kicker: FOUND-SOUND PRODUCTION · THE STREET AS THE DRUM KIT AND THE CHORDS
idea: Turn a field recording into the band. Its own clatter is cut out and layered under house and garage drums, its hiss is tuned into the chords by a bank of resonators, and a phone voice memo is chopped into an emotional hook on top. A journal of four pages, one recording and one line of writing each, builds to a euphoric drop and then lets the street back in. Found-sound dance producers of the 2020s work this way: phone audio, field recordings and journal-like sampling over two-step and four-to-the-floor drums.
controls: 8 slots (voice memo, field recording A, field recording B, kick, clap, hats, keys, sub); groove (two-step garage, four-to-the-floor house, speed-garage bassline, broken), swing, tempo, key; FIELD KIT (the field recording's own hits layered on the drums, sorted low, mid and high); TUNED STREET (six resonators tuned to the chord tones); phone-ness of the voice; a 16-step chop lane you click; chop pitch and density; page length, build bars, euphoria and key lift for the drop; four journal pages (a line of writing, a progression and a field recording each); VJ full-screen mode.
how: Press PLAY. A built-in street recording becomes the groove: its clicks are layered on two-step garage drums, its hiss is tuned to the chords, and a voice-memo phrase is chopped into the hook. Each journal page runs intro, groove, build, an empty beat, the drop and a break. Press J to read the journal page by page (1 to 4 jump to a page), X to go straight to the build, C for new chops, K for the field kit, T for the tuned street and P for the phone voice. Click the chop lane at the bottom to change a chop. Load your own voice memo into slot 1 and two field recordings into slots 2 and 3 (D opens the deck; drag the S and E handles to trim them). F goes full screen for a projector.
try: Walk one street with your phone and record two minutes, then record yourself saying one sentence about the walk. Put the sentence in slot 1 and the street in slot 2, drag the S and E handles to the busiest ten seconds, and turn FIELD KIT up until the street plays the hi-hats.

Make it a journal: record one field recording a day for four days (kettle, bus stop, rain, the pub). Load them into slots 2 and 3 over the week, write one line per day into the journal pages, switch JOURNAL on (J) and record a WAV of the four pages in a row.

Load a held synth note or a choir sample from your Splice library into slot 3, set the page's field to B and TUNED STREET to full: the resonators turn it into chords that follow the progression. Then try the same with plain traffic noise and compare.

manifesto.name: Found-sound production: the field recording as the drum kit and the chords
manifesto.author: Inspired by found-sound house and garage producers of the 2020s (for example Fred again..), and by UK garage
manifesto.where: A working method described in many producer interviews and tutorials; paraphrased here, nothing quoted
ideas: In our words: record your actual life on the phone (a voice memo, a street, a room) and treat it as the raw material of a dance track rather than as decoration.

In our words: field recordings can do more than sit underneath. Their own clicks, footsteps and slams can be cut out and layered with the kick, the clap and the hats, so the place is inside the groove.
In our words: noise holds every pitch. Pass it through narrow filters tuned to the notes of a chord and the hiss of a street or of rain starts to sing that chord.
In our words: a voice memo cut into syllables and pitched to the chord tones becomes an emotional hook, even if the words are hard to make out.
In our words: UK garage swings. The kick skips (the two-step), the hats shuffle, and the bass moves under the chords.
In our words: the euphoric drop works by contrast: thin the track out, hold your breath for one empty beat, then bring everything back wider and brighter, sometimes a tone higher.
In our words: a journal is a good structure. One recording and one line per day, played in order, tells the week.
manifesto.system: Slot 1 is the voice memo, slots 2 and 3 are field recordings. FIELD KIT finds the hits inside the trimmed field recording and sorts them by brightness into low, mid and high, then layers them on the kick, clap and hat steps. TUNED STREET runs the field recording through six narrow resonators set to the current chord's tones, so the noise follows the progression. The chop lane plays one of eight chops of the voice memo per step, pitched to the chord. A journal page runs for PAGE BARS: intro (the street alone), groove, build (high-pass sweep, an accelerating snare roll, a riser and one empty beat), drop (everything, wider, with optional key lift), and break (voice and street). With JOURNAL on, the pages play in order with their own progression and field recording.
manifesto.dubious: The grooves, progressions and sounds are this tool's own. No recording, lyric or arrangement by any producer is used.

title: Return Time
kicker: GENERATIVE SYSTEMS · UNEQUAL TAPE LOOPS, YOUR OWN CARDS, LISTENING AND IGNORING
idea: Tape loops of different lengths never quite line up, so a few simple phrases keep making new combinations, and the moment they all return together can be days or centuries away. This machine runs six loops of unequal length, four of notes and two of your own trimmed sounds, and works out exactly when they will next meet. Each loop is a channel of an imaginary tape studio with its own speed, wear, wow and echo, so the studio itself is the instrument. You write your own prompt cards, the machine draws one every few minutes and acts on it, a gardener lets worn loops fade and plants new ones, and an attention fader moves the music between something to listen to closely and something to leave in the background.
controls: 6 slots (piano, voice pad, glass, low tone, tape loop A, tape loop B); four note loops with their own length (3 to 40 s), speed, level and phrase; two audio tape loops whose length is the trimmed region (drag S and E); return-time readout (when all six loops line up again) and meetings counter; attention fader from IGNORE to LISTEN; tape wear per pass, wow and flutter, saturation, tape echo; gardener on/off and rate; scale and key; density; your own prompt cards (one per line, optional [action] tag), drawn by hand or every N minutes; Gemini writes new cards from a mood (optional, your own key).
how: Press PLAY. Six reels start turning together, each a different length, and the readout tells you when they will all line up again. Drag the ATTENTION fader (or press C to listen closely, B to let it sit in the background) and hear the music come forward or recede. Press O to draw one of your prompt cards; the machine acts on it. Edit the cards in the side panel: one per line, with a tag like [slower], [thin], [plant] or [echo] if you want the machine to act. G turns the gardener on and off; N plants a new phrase; P prunes one; A starts every loop together again (realign). Load your own sounds with the deck (D): slots 5 and 6 are true tape loops, so trimming them with S and E changes the loop length and the return time.
try: Load a long, soft recording (a room, rain, a held chord from your Splice folder) into slot 5 and a shorter one into slot 6. Drag the S and E handles on each and watch the RETURN TIME readout jump from minutes to years. Find a trim where it reads more than a year, then press A to realign and let it run while you do something else.

Write six cards of your own before you press PLAY, about the room you are in (for example: 'the radiator is the bass [low]', 'someone just came in, get quieter [ignore]'). Set CARD EVERY to 2 minutes and record a WAV of whatever the cards make of the evening.

Put four short one-shots from your own library into slots 1 to 4 (a pluck, a breath, a bell, a low hit). Turn WEAR up and leave the GARDENER on for ten minutes: write down which planted phrase you missed when it faded, then plant it back by hand with the number key.

manifesto.name: Generative tape loops: unequal lengths, your own cards, the studio as instrument
manifesto.short: Unequal tape loops and the return time
manifesto.author: Inspired by Brian Eno's ambient and generative working methods
manifesto.where: Ambient and generative records and liner notes of the late 1970s; his talks on the studio as a compositional tool
ideas: Tape loops of different lengths never quite line up, so a few simple phrases keep making new combinations, and the moment they all return together can be days or centuries away.
In the late 1970s ambient records were made by setting loops of unequal, unrelated lengths running together and letting the combinations happen, instead of writing every note in order.
The studio was treated as an instrument in its own right: speed, echo, saturation and tape wear became parts of the composition, not just ways of recording it.
A deck of prompt cards, each a short suggestion to act on when stuck, was used to break habits in the studio. Here you write your own cards: no published card text is used or imitated.
In our words: ambient music was meant to reward close listening but also to be easy to ignore, so the same piece could sit in the background or be the centre of attention.
In our words: a generative piece is more like a garden than an architecture: you set conditions, plant, prune and let it grow, rather than building every part.
In our words: the return time of unequal loops is simple arithmetic: it is the least common multiple of their lengths, which grows astonishingly fast as the lengths become less related.
manifesto.system: Four note loops each hold a short phrase (one to four notes from the chosen scale) at fixed places in a loop of their own length; two audio loops play the trimmed region of slots 5 and 6, so their length is the trim divided by the speed. All six start together on PLAY or R. The return time is the least common multiple of the six effective lengths, rounded to tenths of a second, counted from that start. Each pass wears the tape: level and brightness fall by WEAR, and a loop that is nearly gone is replanted by the GARDENER with a new phrase; the gardener also adds or removes single notes now and then. ATTENTION changes how often notes play, how soft their attacks are, the overall brightness and whether small ornaments appear. A card's [tag] acts on the machine: slower, faster, thin, plant, prune, reverse, silence, low, echo, dry, wow, listen, ignore, realign. Wow and flutter drift each note's pitch; saturation and a tape echo with a wavering delay time colour the whole mix.
manifesto.dubious: The phrases, loop lengths, sounds and every card are this tool's own; no record, loop length or published card text is reproduced. The least common multiple is exact for the rounded lengths, but real tape loops drift, so they would never quite meet.

title: Circle Walk
kicker: MUSIC THEORY · THE CIRCLE OF FIFTHS, WALKED, TUNED AND HEARD
idea: Arrange the twelve keys in a circle where each step is a perfect fifth and the whole of Western harmony becomes a map: neighbouring keys share all but one note, relative minors share a key signature, and the strongest chord progressions move round the circle one fifth at a time. This instrument walks that map with your own sounds. Pick a walk (the diatonic chain of falling fifths, two-five-one chains, a tour of all twelve dominants, or a pivot-chord modulation to a neighbouring key) and hear every chord voice-led to the next by the smallest moves. Switch to pure fifths and the circle stops closing: after twelve perfect fifths you arrive about a quarter of a semitone sharp, the gap that equal temperament spreads around the circle.
controls: 7 slots (keys C4, bass C2, lead C5, pad C4, kick, hat, snare/rim); four walks (falling fifths in the key, ii-V-I chains, the twelve-dominant tour, pivot modulation); key (on the circle) and major or relative minor; modulate after each lap (stay, flatwards, sharpwards, to a random neighbour); sevenths or triads; harmonic-minor V; chord length; equal or pure-fifth tuning with drift readout and comma reset; groove (bossa, brushes, four, none); swing; guide-tone melody amount; keys, bass, lead, pad and drum levels.
how: Press PLAY. The walker moves round the circle: each chord's root lights up and a line joins it to the last, while the panel names the chord, its Roman numeral, the key and its signature. Press 1 to 4 to change walk, M for the relative minor, and click any key on the circle to jump there. Set MODULATE to flatwards or sharpwards and the key moves one step each lap, adding one flat or one sharp. Press T to switch to pure fifths and watch the drift readout grow as the walk goes round; K resets the comma. Load your own keys, bass and lead sounds with the deck (D); slots say which note they should be.
try: Load a single sustained note from your own library (a Rhodes, a sung 'ooh', a synth pad) into slot 1, trim it with the S and E handles to the steadiest part, and listen to the FALLING FIFTHS walk with SEVENTHS on. Sing along with the lead line: it only ever uses each chord's third and seventh, and you will hear how they slide by a semitone into the next chord.

manifesto.name: The circle of fifths: keys, relative minors and progressions by fifths
manifesto.author: Nikolai Diletskii's Grammatika (1679) and Johann David Heinichen's Der General-Bass in der Composition (1728); the Pythagorean comma (ancient Greek tuning theory)
manifesto.year: 1679 and 1728 (circle diagrams); about 500 BC onwards (the comma)
manifesto.where: Diletskii's treatise on composition, written in Moscow; Heinichen's thorough-bass treatise, Dresden
ideas: Arrange the twelve keys in a circle where each step is a perfect fifth and the whole of Western harmony becomes a map: neighbouring keys share all but one note, relative minors share a key signature, and the strongest chord progressions move round the circle one fifth at a time.

Seventeenth-century treatises drew the keys in a circle of fifths to show how a composer could move from any key to any other; an eighteenth-century thorough-bass manual drew a circle of major and minor keys side by side.

Moving clockwise adds one sharp to the key signature; moving anticlockwise adds one flat. Every major key has a relative minor three steps clockwise round the circle (or a minor third below) that shares its notes.

In our words: a root moving down a fifth (or up a fourth) is the strongest progression in tonal music. Chains of falling fifths, such as two-five-one or the diatonic cycle through every chord of the key, drive harmony forward.

In our words: when chords move by fifths, their thirds and sevenths move by step: the seventh of one chord falls a semitone to become the third of the next. These guide tones are the smallest, smoothest line through the changes.
In our words: a pivot chord belongs to two neighbouring keys at once, so it can carry the music from one key into the next without a jolt.

In our words: twelve perfect fifths overshoot seven octaves by a small interval, the Pythagorean comma (about 23.5 cents). Equal temperament narrows every fifth very slightly so the circle closes; pure fifths turn the circle into a spiral.
manifesto.system: Every pitch is stored as a position on the line of fifths. In equal tuning a position p sounds 7p semitones above C (folded into one octave); in pure tuning it sounds 7.01955p semitones, so a walk that goes all the way round the circle comes back 23.46 cents away from where it started, and the drift readout shows how far you are from the key where you last pressed comma reset. Chord tones are also positions on the line (major third +4, minor third -3, fifth +1, minor seventh -2, major seventh +5, diminished fifth -6), so pure tuning gives Pythagorean chords with bright, wide thirds. Each new chord is voiced by trying every inversion in two octaves and picking the one with the least total movement from the last. FALLING FIFTHS plays the diatonic cycle (I IV vii iii vi ii V I, or i iv VII III VI ii V i in minor). TWO-FIVE-ONE plays ii V I. THE TOUR plays dominant sevenths on all twelve roots in falling fifths. PIVOT plays I, then the chord shared by this key and its neighbour, then V and I of the new key. After each lap MODULATE can move the key one step round the circle. The lead plays guide tones (thirds and sevenths).
manifesto.dubious: The walks, voicings, melodies and grooves are this tool's own. The two-five-one is common practice and belongs to everyone. Historians debate who drew the first circle of fifths; we give the two best-known early treatises.

title: Mycelial Network
kicker: NATURE · FUNGAL THREADS THAT JOIN A FOREST, PLAYED AS A NETWORK OF SOUNDS
idea: Under a forest floor, fungal threads branch, fuse and wrap the roots of the trees, trading minerals and water for sugar, so the forest is joined by a living network you never see. This instrument grows one. Five trees are five of your sounds; threads grow out from them, branch and fuse where they meet, and once two trees are joined a pulse sent from one reaches the other after a delay set by the length of the path. The network becomes the score: rhythms come from distances, a well-fed web fruits into mushrooms that ring out as chords, and drought makes it die back to silence.
controls: 7 slots (five trees: bell, wood, low string, voice, pluck; forest floor grains; fruiting chime); growth rate, branching, fusion distance; drought (die-back) and FEED (a growth burst); pulse speed along the threads, reach, how often the trees pulse (mother tree only, or every tree on its own period), relay chance (a tree that receives a pulse sends its own); hum of the branch points (grains); fruiting threshold; scale and key; quantise to the grid or free time; levels; click to drop a spore or fire a tree.
how: Press PLAY. The network has already started to grow from the five trees. A pulse leaves the first tree every couple of beats and travels along the threads in red; wherever it reaches another tree, that tree sounds. Click any tree to send a pulse from it, or click empty ground to drop a spore and start a new thread. Press E to feed the network (a growth burst), raise DROUGHT to make it die back, and X to clear it and start again from spores. When enough trees are joined and the threads are busy, a mushroom fruits and rings out. Load your own sounds into the trees with the deck (D).
try: Load five sounds recorded on one walk (a gate, a branch snapping, a bird, a footstep in leaves, your own voice saying where you are) into the five trees and switch PULSES to 'every tree'. Let the network grow for a few minutes: the rhythm you hear is the shape of the web between the places.

Set RELAY to about 0.6 and drop the pulse rate low, then click one tree. Listen to the message spread through the forest as each tree passes it on. Turn SPEED down to hear it travel slowly; trim each sample short with the S and E handles so the cascade stays clear.
Feed the network (E) until it fruits, then raise DROUGHT slowly to 0.8 and record a WAV as it dies back and goes quiet. Lower DROUGHT again and hear it regrow from what is left.

manifesto.name: Mycelial networks: the fungal web beneath a forest
manifesto.author: Inspired by research on mycorrhizal fungi and fungal growth
manifesto.where: Field studies of carbon moving between trees through shared fungi (from 1997), and laboratory studies of how fungal networks grow and fuse
ideas: Under a forest floor, fungal threads branch, fuse and wrap the roots of the trees, trading minerals and water for sugar, so the forest is joined by a living network you never see.
A fungus is mostly a mycelium: a web of microscopic threads called hyphae that grow at their tips, branch and spread through soil and wood. The mushroom is only its short-lived fruit.
Where two threads meet they can fuse (anastomosis), turning a branching tree of threads into a true network with loops and shortcuts.
Most plants live with mycorrhizal fungi: the fungus brings water and minerals to the root and takes sugars made by the plant in return.
Field experiments from 1997 found traces of carbon moving between trees through shared fungi, and a popular nickname compared the forest to a web.
In our words: networks thicken where they carry most and thin where they are not used; laboratory fungi have even been shown to rebuild efficient transport networks between food sources.
In our words: thinking of a forest as a network, not as separate trees competing, changes how you see a wood, even where the details are still argued about.
manifesto.system: Five trees are fixed points in the soil, one per sample slot. Hyphal tips grow from them in short steps, wandering a little and branching now and then; when a tip comes within FUSION DISTANCE of a thread from another lineage the two fuse and the tip stops. Pulses leave the mother tree (or every tree, each on its own period) and travel along the threads at SPEED, using the shortest path, out to REACH. When a pulse arrives at another tree, that tree sounds a note from the scale (its own degree plus the number of fusions on the way), so rhythm comes from distance. Branch points it passes hum with tiny grains of the forest floor slot. Threads that carry pulses gather nutrient; when at least FRUIT trees are joined and a branch point is rich enough, a mushroom fruits there with a rising chord from the fruiting slot and spores start new threads. DROUGHT slows growth and makes unused tips die back; FEED gives a burst of growth. With QUANTISE on, every arrival snaps to the nearest sixteenth.
manifesto.dubious: Real fungal networks grow over weeks and any signals between trees take hours or days; here time is enormously compressed. Popular claims that trees deliberately share food, warn each other or nurture their young through 'mother trees' are contested: recent reviews argue the field evidence is weaker than popular accounts suggest. This tool uses the network as a picture of connection, not as proof of tree communication.

title: Regulating Lines
kicker: ART MANIFESTO · PURISM: STANDARD OBJECTS, REGULATING LINES, A MUSIC OF ORDER
idea: After the fragments of Cubism, a 1918 Paris manifesto asked for an art of order: plain standard objects such as bottles, glasses, pipes and guitars, perfected by use like good machines, arranged on regulating lines of exact proportion and painted in a calm, ranked scale of colours. This instrument makes that still life playable. Six standard objects are six of your sounds; where you place each one on the canvas sets when it plays, how high it is sets its pitch and how wide sets how long it lasts. Regulating lines (halves, thirds, the golden section or the square root of two) pull every object into proportion, objects that share a contour sound together, and the colour scale decides each object's character.
controls: 7 slots (bottle, glass, pipe, guitar, jug C2, plate, machine pulse); drag objects to move them (they snap to the regulating lines), drag the right edge to change length; four proportion systems (halves, thirds, golden section, root two); snap on or off; marriage of contours (overlapping objects play together); constants (married objects tuned to unisons, fourths and fifths); colour scale per object (the calm major scale, the dynamic scale, the transitional scale); canvas length in beats; tempo; key and scale; legato; the hand (human timing) versus the machine; machine pulse level; ORDER snaps everything, SCATTER throws it into cubist disorder.
how: Press PLAY. A playhead sweeps the still life from left to right and each object sounds as it is reached: higher objects play higher notes, wider ones last longer. Drag an object to move it and watch it snap to the red regulating lines; drag its right edge to stretch it. Press G to change the proportion system and O to put every object in order on the new lines; X scatters them into cubist disorder for comparison. Click an object and press C to change its colour (and so its character), 1 to 6 to add a new object, Delete to remove one. Load your own standard sounds (a bottle tapped, a glass, a pipe, a guitar) with the deck (D).
try: Record six everyday objects from your kitchen or desk (tap a bottle, ring a glass, knock a mug, pluck a rubber band) and load one into each object slot. Trim each with the S and E handles to a single clean hit, then press O with the GOLDEN SECTION system and listen to your kitchen in proportion.

Build a still life with HALVES, record a WAV, then press G until you reach GOLDEN SECTION and press O. Record again. The objects are the same and only the proportions changed: which version feels more like a groove, and which like architecture?

Turn CONSTANTS on and drag two objects so they overlap. They marry, play together and tune to a fourth or fifth. Then colour one from the dynamic scale (citron, orange, vermilion) and hear it push forward against the calm earth colours.

manifesto.name: Purism: After Cubism (1918)
manifesto.author: Amédée Ozenfant and Charles-Édouard Jeanneret (later known as Le Corbusier)
manifesto.where: The manifesto Après le cubisme (Paris, 1918) and the journal L'Esprit Nouveau (1920 to 1925)
ideas: After the fragments of Cubism, a 1918 Paris manifesto asked for an art of order: plain standard objects such as bottles, glasses, pipes and guitars, perfected by use like good machines, arranged on regulating lines of exact proportion and painted in a calm, ranked scale of colours.
In our words: the authors felt Cubism had become decorative and fragmented, and wanted painting to be as clear, exact and universal as engineering.

In our words: everyday objects shaped by long use (a wine bottle, a glass, a pipe, a jug, a guitar) are 'standard' or type objects: their forms have been refined by use until nothing is extra, like a well-made machine part.
In our words: a composition should be ordered by regulating lines, simple geometry such as diagonals, right angles and golden-section divisions, that fix where things go.
In our words: in a Purist still life the objects overlap and share outlines, so one contour belongs to two objects at once (sometimes called a marriage of contours).

In our words: colours were ranked. A calm, constructive major scale of ochres, earth reds, white, black and ultramarine; a dynamic, agitating scale of citron yellow, orange and vermilion; and a transitional scale of madder, emerald and lakes.
In our words: the aim was a universal art based on constants that anyone, anywhere, would feel the same way, rather than on personal expression.
manifesto.system: The canvas is one loop of N beats. An object's left edge is its onset, its width is its length, and the height of its centre is its pitch in the chosen scale (the jug sounds two octaves lower). With SNAP on, every edge snaps to the regulating lines of the chosen system: HALVES (sixteenths of the canvas), THIRDS (twelfths), GOLDEN SECTION (the canvas cut at 0.382 and 0.618, and each part cut again the same way) or ROOT TWO (cuts at 0.293 and 0.707, repeated). Golden and root-two lines make rhythms that are proportional but not on the usual grid. Objects whose outlines overlap are married: the later one plays at the earlier one's onset, and with CONSTANTS on its pitch is moved to the nearest unison, fourth or fifth above the other. Colour sets character: the major scale is warm and steady (filtered, full length), the dynamic scale is bright and short with an accent, the transitional scale is soft and drifts into reverb and echo. The machine pulse marks the beats; THE HAND adds human timing.
manifesto.dubious: Purism was a painting movement; it had no music. The sounds, proportions-to-rhythm mapping and the colour-to-timbre mapping are this tool's own reading. The manifesto text is in copyright and is only paraphrased here.

title: Resample Chain
kicker: FOUND-SOUND PRODUCER METHOD · BOUNCE IT, RE-CHOP IT, LET THE SONG EAT ITSELF
idea: A phone voice memo, a street recording and a few drums become a house or garage track in five sections: intro, verse, build, drop and break. The twist is the bounce. At the end of every section the instrument records its own mix into a ninth slot, and the next section chops that bounce instead of (or as well as) the original memo, so each pass is a copy of a copy: warmer, darker and more like a tape you carried around. A snare roll, a rising riser and a deliberate one-beat gap lead into a drop built from your own vocal chops, tuned to the chords. Everything is editable and every sound is yours.
controls: 9 slots (voice memo, room or street, kick, clap, hat, chord stab, bass, riser, bounce); five sections with adjustable length, jump or hold; groove (four-to-the-floor, two-step garage, broken); tempo, swing, key and chord loop; sample root so chops are tuned to the chords; chop density, chop length and tuning mode; hook re-roll; bounce mix (how much comes from the bounce), copy wear (how much each pass darkens) and auto-bounce; sidechain pump; build roll and gap; levels for drums, chords, bass, chops and room; VJ cassette-reel visuals.
how: Press PLAY. The tape counts through the sections of Side A. Press 1 to 5 to jump to a section, N for the next one, P to hold (loop) the current one. B bounces the last section into slot 9 right now, and H writes a new hook from slices of the active source. Load a voice memo into slot 1 (the deck, D), a street or room recording into slot 2, and trim each with the S and E handles. Set SAMPLE ROOT to the note your memo is sung on so the chops are tuned to the chords. Turn BOUNCE MIX up and each section chops the last, a copy of a copy.
try: Record a 5 to 10 second voice note on your phone (humming a line, or saying something you want to remember), load it into slot 1 and trim it with the S and E handles to the best breath. Set SAMPLE ROOT to the note you hummed, choose the VI-IV-I-V chord loop and play. Listen for the drop: the same voice, now tuned to the chords.

Record a minute of a street, a kitchen or a train into slot 2 and set the ROOM level up in the intro and break. Then set BOUNCE MIX to about 70 per cent and let two or three passes run: by the second drop the chops are made from the earlier mix, with drums and chords inside them.

Turn BUILD GAP on and set CHOP LENGTH short, then record a WAV of one build and drop. Load that WAV back into slot 1, trim the most interesting two seconds and press H until the hook feels like a song you have heard before. This is the whole method: keep bouncing and keep choosing.

manifesto.name: Found-sound production: the resample chain
manifesto.author: Inspired by found-audio house and garage producers of the 2020s (no quotes, no copied patterns or audio)
manifesto.year: 2020s, from older sampling and tape-bounce practice
manifesto.where: Bedroom and laptop production, with ideas from tape bouncing in 1970s and 1980s studios and from hip-hop and garage sampling
ideas: In our words: found-sound producers treat a phone recording as a first draft of a song. A voice note, a street recording or a bit of speech is the seed, and the track is grown by cutting, tuning and repeating it.

In our words: a bounce is a recording of your own mix. Bouncing and then chopping the bounce gives you new sounds that already carry the groove, the room and the chords inside them, and each generation adds a little wear.
In our words: a euphoric drop is built from contrast. The build raises pitch, speeds up the roll and removes weight, a short gap empties the music, and the drop returns every part at once.
In our words: a vocal chop becomes an instrument when it is tuned to the chords. The same slice can be a root, a third or a fifth depending on what sits under it.
In our words: house and garage grooves differ mainly in where the kick and snare fall and how the hats swing: four steady kicks, or a skipping two-step.
manifesto.system: Sixteen steps per bar, with swing on the odd steps. Each section runs for a set number of bars; the chord loop changes every bar. The chops come from slices found by the onset detector inside your trimmed region, and each slice is pitched to the nearest chord tone relative to SAMPLE ROOT. In the build, a snare roll doubles its rate each bar, the riser slot is stretched up two octaves, a noise sweep opens, and in the last half bar everything stops (the gap). The drop brings back kick, bass, chords and the hook. At the end of each section the tool records its own output (a tap on the master) and puts the last section in slot 9; BOUNCE MIX decides how many chops come from it, and COPY WEAR darkens its filter each pass. Slot 9 is a normal slot, so you can trim, reverse and pitch it.
manifesto.dubious: This describes a general method used by many producers, not any one person's recipe. The patterns and chord loops here are the tool's own. Nothing is copied from any recording.

title: Learned Garden
kicker: GENERATIVE SYSTEMS · A GARDEN THAT LEARNS YOUR HABITS, SEASONS AND WEEDS
idea: Plant a short phrase and a garden of independent players learns its habits: which note tends to follow which. Each plant then wanders through that map at its own pace, so the music never repeats but always sounds like its seed. You tend it rather than build it: water it with your own notes and it learns your habits, let it feed on itself and it slowly settles into favourite paths, let a few weeds in and it surprises you, prune it back and it forgets. A slow season cycle thins and thickens the garden over minutes, and an attention fader moves it between music to listen to and music to ignore.
controls: 7 slots (pluck, bell, pad, low voice, texture, seed drop, your hand); seed phrase (scale degrees you can type); key and scale; learned transition map (first or second order memory); temperature (how adventurous); weeds; habit (how much it learns from itself); plant and prune plants; speed; season length in minutes or a fixed season; attention (ignore to listen); your notes on the keyboard, the map or MIDI teach it; levels for plants, pad, your hand and texture.
how: Press PLAY. Five plants start from the seed phrase and wander, each at its own pace. The left map shows what the garden has learned: brighter squares are habits, and each plant's current step is a dot. Press A to L (or click a column on the map) to play a note of your own and teach the garden that step; do a short phrase twice and listen for it in the garden. P plants a new plant, X prunes one, W lets weeds in, and the attention fader moves from background to foreground. Load your own sounds into the slots in the deck (D) and trim them with the S and E handles.
try: Load one clean, sustained note (a Rhodes, a bowed note, a sung vowel) into slot 1 and one short bell or pluck into slot 2, trimming each with the S and E handles. Type your own seed phrase (for example 0 4 2 5 4 7), press PLAY, and watch which habits the map learns.

Set ATTENTION low, HABIT high and WEEDS to nothing, and let the garden run for five minutes while you do something else. It will settle into a few favourite paths. Then raise WEEDS and press X to prune, and listen to it open up again.

Play a short phrase of your own on the keys four or five times and then stop. Load a field recording into slot 5 for the texture and record a WAV. The same phrase, now in the plants' voices, is your habit played back by a garden.

manifesto.name: Generative systems: gardening, not architecture
manifesto.author: Inspired by generative-music practice since the 1990s, and by Andrey Markov's chains of probabilities (1906 to 1913)
manifesto.year: 1990s to now; Markov chains from 1906 to 1913
manifesto.where: Generative and ambient music, and the mathematics of chains of linked chances
ideas: In our words: in generative music you do not write the notes, you set up a system that writes them. The skill is in choosing the seed and the rules, then listening.
In our words: a Markov chain is a table of how likely each state is to follow another. Learn the table from a phrase and you can generate endless music that behaves like it, without ever copying it.
In our words: a garden metaphor suits this. You plant, you water, you prune, you let things go wild in places. You do not control a plant's every leaf, and you do not need to.
In our words: ambient music can be listened to closely or left in the background. A garden of slow, unequal cycles rewards both: close up you hear the habits, and far away you hear a mood.
In our words: seasons give a long arc without a score. The garden thickens, brightens, thins and rests, so the piece has a shape that no-one drew.
manifesto.system: Your seed phrase is read as scale degrees. Every step from one note to the next is counted in a table (and every pair-to-next in a second table when MEMORY is 2). Each plant has its own register, voice and pace (they are deliberately unequal), keeps its last note or two, and picks the next from the table weighted by how often it was seen. TEMPERATURE flattens or sharpens that choice. WEEDS adds notes that are not in the table. HABIT feeds a small amount of each generated step back into the table, so favourite paths grow. Notes you play are counted heavily. The season wheel scales how many plants are awake, how often they play, how bright the filter is and whether the garden sits an octave lower. ATTENTION lowers level and brightness for background listening and, when high, makes the garden recite its seed slowly now and then.
manifesto.dubious: The mapping of probabilities to plants and seasons is this tool's own. Markov's work was on chains of letters in a poem, not music; its use for composition came later and is a general technique, so no one person's piece is used here.

title: Song Form Blocks
kicker: MUSIC THEORY · SONG FORM: TWELVE BARS, AABA, VERSE AND CHORUS, THE HOOK, CALL AND RESPONSE
idea: Most songs are built from a handful of blocks. The twelve-bar blues is a three-line chord pattern that has carried countless songs. AABA is a thirty-two-bar form: a tune twice, a contrasting bridge, the tune again. Verse and chorus put a talking section against a singing one. This instrument lets you pick a form and see it as a row of printed blocks, then plays it with your own sounds: a band (keys, bass, drums), a hook that you can re-roll, and a call-and-response conversation in which one voice makes a short phrase and another answers it. Change the form, the swing or the way the answer is made and you hear how structure shapes feeling.
controls: 8 slots (keys, bass, kick, snare or brush, ride or hat, caller, responder, organ); five forms (12-bar blues, minor 12-bar, 8-bar blues, 32-bar AABA, verse-chorus-bridge); key, tempo and swing from straight to shuffle; chord richness (triads, sevenths, ninths); quick change and turnaround for the blues; comping style (stabs, sustained, charleston, shuffle); bass style (walking, root and fifth, boogie); note set (minor blues, major blues, major); hook strength and length; call length (one or two bars) and answer style (echo, mirror, fifth above, resolve, free); blue-note bend; levels; VJ chord blocks.
how: Press PLAY. The page shows the whole form as a grid of wood-type blocks, one per bar, with the chord on each and the bar that is playing lit. Press 1 to 5 to choose a form. The caller plays a short hook and the responder answers it, and every four bars the pair swap roles. H writes a new hook, S flips between straight and shuffle feel, Q toggles the quick change in the blues. Load a short note into the keys slot and a bass note into the bass slot (D opens the deck), and trim each with the S and E handles. Change the answer style to hear the same call answered four ways.
try: Load one clear, short pitched sound (a piano note, a guitar pluck, a vocal 'hey') into slot 6 (responder) and a related sound into slot 5 (caller). Choose the 12-BAR BLUES, set swing to shuffle, trim both with the S and E handles to the cleanest part, and notice how the form tells you when to call and when to answer.

Choose AABA and listen only for the bridge. Put your most unusual sound into the organ slot and turn the organ up. Notice how the bridge feels like a different place, and how glad you are to come back to the tune.

Set the answer style to MIRROR, hook strength to high and press H until you find a hook you could sing. Record a WAV. Then change only the form and record again. Same hook, different structure: which feels like a complete story?

manifesto.name: Song form: the blues, AABA and verse-chorus, with the hook and call and response
manifesto.author: Anonymous folk and popular traditions; the blues of the early 1900s; the popular song of the 1920s to 1950s
manifesto.year: Early 1900s to 1950s (blues); 1920s to 1950s (AABA); 1950s to now (verse and chorus)
manifesto.where: African American blues and work-song traditions; American popular song and the music publishers of the early twentieth century; rock and pop songwriting
ideas: In our words: the twelve-bar blues is a three-line shape. The first line sets out the home chord for four bars, the second moves away to the fourth chord and returns, and the third is the turn that heads for a close. A singer states a line, repeats it, and answers with the third.

In our words: AABA is a thirty-two-bar form of four eight-bar sections. The tune is played twice, then a bridge goes somewhere else harmonically, then the tune returns, so the return feels like coming home.
In our words: verse-and-chorus form separates the story from the sing-along. Verses change their words while the chorus stays the same, and a bridge comes late to give a change of view.
In our words: a hook is a short, repeated phrase that sticks in the memory. It usually has a clear rhythm and a small range, and it comes back often enough to be recognised.

In our words: call and response is a conversation: one voice states a phrase and another answers it with an echo, a mirror, a reply or a resolution. It is common in many musical traditions and underlies the blues line.
manifesto.system: Each form is a list of sections, and each section is a list of bars with one chord per bar, taken from the tool's own tables. The band plays what you chose for each bar: the keys comp, the bass line and the drums on an eight-note grid whose off-beats are pushed late by the swing control (0 is straight, 1 is triplet shuffle). The hook is generated from the note set with a small range and a clear rhythm. In each phrase the caller plays the hook; the responder then answers it with the style you picked: an echo, a mirror (turned upside down), a fifth higher, a resolution (the same rhythm that ends on the key note), or a new phrase. BLUE BEND slides the flat third and flat fifth up into pitch. In the major forms notes on strong beats snap to the chord. In the verse-chorus form the verses are sparse, the choruses full and the bridge drops out the drums.
manifesto.dubious: These forms are common traditions, not any one composer's. The chord tables, hooks and rhythms here are generated by the tool itself and are not copied from any song.

title: Standing Waves
live_label: ▶ Play Standing Loops, the stand-alone sample looper and mixer in this style ↗
kicker: NATURE · THE HARMONIC SERIES, STIFF STRINGS AND SAND ON A VIBRATING PLATE
idea: Every pitched sound that rings is made of a stack of pure tones whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of a lowest one: the harmonic series. A string, a pipe and a voice all behave this way, and the series gives us the octave, the fifth, the major third and the strange, flat seventh. This instrument makes the series audible. A bank of sixteen ringing filters is tuned to the multiples of a low note. Your own sounds are fed through it, so they ring like a struck plate. A melody walks up and down the series in pure, just tuning. On the screen a plate of sand shows the pattern each tone would draw, and you can switch tones on and off and make the plate stiffer so the tones drift out of tune.

how: Press PLAY. Your sounds are fed into sixteen tuned resonators, so everything rings on the low note you chose. Click the spectrum bars on the right to switch harmonics on, off, or to any level, and watch the sand figure change. Raise STIFFNESS and the upper tones go sharp, as in a real metal string. Turn on the BOW to ring the filters with a steady sound (a held breath or a bowed tone), or set STRIKE to tap them with short sounds. Load any sound into the melody slot (D opens the deck) and trim its S and E handles. Press F for the full-screen sand plate.

Each hit rings out a chord of harmonics tuned to your low note. Click the spectrum to keep only the odd harmonics, then only the even ones, and hear how the colour changes.

Put a long vocal note or a held pad into slot 3 (BOW, loops) and turn the bow level up. Use FUNDAMENTAL MOVEMENT: UP A FIFTH so that the resonators move between roots every few bars. Record a WAV: it is your voice turned into a tuned, glassy plate.

Raise STIFFNESS slowly with a bell or a piano note in the melody slot, then change TUNING between JUST and EQUAL. The seventh harmonic is clearly flat against a piano key. Which version do you prefer, and why does the odd one sound so good?

manifesto.name: Standing waves and the harmonic series
manifesto.author: Physics and the acoustics of strings, pipes and plates
manifesto.year: Ancient observation; plates studied from the late 1700s
manifesto.where: The physics of vibrating strings, air columns and plates; the history of musical tuning
ideas: In our words: a vibrating string splits itself into halves, thirds, quarters and more, all at once. The tones this makes are the harmonics, with frequencies of one, two, three, four times the lowest.
In our words: the ratios 2 to 1, 3 to 2 and 5 to 4 are the octave, the fifth and the major third, so these intervals are built into the physics of sound rather than made up by us.
In our words: the seventh harmonic and the eleventh do not match any note on a piano. They sit between the keys, which is why 'just' tuned melodies can sound pure and strange.
In our words: stiff strings and plates do not ring in perfect multiples. Their upper tones are pushed sharp, which is why bells, gongs and steel plates sound different from a plucked cord.
In our words: sand scattered on a vibrating plate runs to the places that do not move and draws lines between them. Each tone makes its own pattern of nodes, so you can see a standing wave.
manifesto.system: The sixteen resonators are band-pass filters at the multiples of the fundamental. Each frequency is the harmonic number times the fundamental, times the square root of 1 plus the stiffness times the number squared, a standard way of modelling a stiff string. Each harmonic has a level you can paint, multiplied by a tilt that makes higher ones quieter. Sound from the melody voice, the strike slot and the bow slot is sent into the bank, and the bank's output is mixed with the original. The melody picks harmonic numbers within the range you set and tunes them exactly (just) or rounds them to the nearest key (equal). The sand figure adds up one simple wave pattern per harmonic and draws the places where the total is close to zero.
manifesto.dubious: The sand figure is a stylised drawing from simple formulae, not a physical simulation of a real plate. The resonator bank is a handy approximation of a vibrating body.

title: Zero Field
kicker: ART MANIFESTO · ZERO: A COUNTDOWN TO A ZONE OF SILENCE, THEN A NEW BEGINNING
idea: In the late 1950s a group of artists in Düsseldorf took the name ZERO. They borrowed it from the countdown before a rocket launch, and from the idea of a zone of silence from which something new can begin. Their work favoured light, vibration, repetition and pure, quiet structure over expression and story. This instrument turns that attitude into sound. Seven repeating voices of your own sounds make a calm, even field. A countdown removes them one by one, down to zero, where only a single quiet tone and silence remain. Then the field begins again, perhaps in a new key. Small controls let the voices drift out of step, wobble in pitch like light on a surface, or lock tightly in time.

how: Press PLAY. Seven voices repeat at their own speeds in an even field, and the big number shows the countdown. Every few bars the number drops, a voice leaves and the field gets quieter and duller. At zero only a low tone is left; then the numbers return. Click a colour bar to mute a voice. Drift makes the voices slip out of step slowly, so the pattern shifts like a moire. Load a sound into the pulse slot (D opens the deck) and trim its S and E handles. N skips to the next stage, Z jumps to the zero zone, P holds the countdown, and F opens the full-screen test card.
try: Put a single plain sound, such as one hand clap or one sine-like note, into slots 1 and 4 and set the note set to ONE NOTE. Trim both with the S and E handles to the cleanest part, then listen to what happens when nothing changes except the countdown.

Load a long, soft room recording into slot 8 (zero tone, loops). Set the zone of silence to 16 beats. It is now the only thing that plays at zero: a place of quiet you made from your own sound. Record a WAV and use the quiet part as the intro for another track.

Choose the MOIRE pattern set, raise DRIFT to about halfway and put your own tapped, plucked and shaken sounds in slots 2, 3 and 6. Let it run through three countdowns. Notice how the pattern never repeats exactly, even though each voice is perfectly regular.

manifesto.name: ZERO: the countdown, the zone of silence and the new beginning

manifesto.where: Düsseldorf, Germany; later an international network of artists working with light, motion and monochrome
ideas: In our words: the name was taken from a countdown, the moment when everything is counted down to nothing and the launch can begin.

In our words: the group preferred light, vibration, repetition and calm structure to personal expression, gesture and storytelling.
In our words: it published a small magazine in the late 1950s and early 1960s and held evening shows in which works were shown for a single night.

In stage k, the number of voices heard is k divided by the count, rounded up, and the level and brightness fall with it. At zero only the zero tone sounds, with a long fade in and out. title: Hold and Release
kicker: FOUND-SOUND PRODUCTION · HOLD THE BUILD, RELEASE THE DROP, STACK THE CROWD
idea: In much found-audio dance music the best moment is not a sound but a pause: tension is held, then released. This instrument puts that moment under your hand. Hold a key and the track builds: the kick falls away, the snare rolls faster, a filter climbs, your voice memo stutters in shorter and shorter slices and everything rises in pitch. Let go and, on the next bar line, there is a breath of silence and then the drop, where one voice of yours becomes a crowd singing along. The longer you hold, the bigger it lands.

Let go: the drop lands on the next bar after a short silence. Load a voice memo into slot 1 (D opens the deck) and trim it with the S and E handles to the phrase you want to chop. N picks new chop positions for the hook, X drops at the next bar, Z resets, F opens the full-screen board.
try: Record a short phone voice memo of a phrase (a spoken line, a hum, a laugh) and load it into slot 1. Trim the S and E handles to one clean word. Use NEW HOOK a few times until the chops feel like a melody, then hold HOLD for a full build and let go.

Load a minute of street, kitchen or train noise into slot 5 (field recording). Set BUILD to 8 bars and SILENCE to 2 beats, then hold through the whole build: notice how the quiet space before the drop makes the field recording feel huge when the kick returns.
Set CROWD VOICES to 7 and CHORD VOICING to 0 (a unison gang), then to 1 (a choir on chord tones). Record a WAV of each and compare: the same single voice becomes a stadium or a church.

manifesto.name: Found-sound production: hold the build, release the drop, stack the crowd
manifesto.author: Inspired by found-audio house and garage producers of the 2020s (no quotes, no copied patterns or audio)
manifesto.year: 2020s, from older dance-music tension and release
manifesto.where: Phone voice memos, field recordings and club music
ideas: In our words: the drop works because of what is taken away first. The kick leaves, the filter closes the low end off, and the ear starts to ask for it back.
In our words: a build speeds things up on purpose: snare rolls double in rate, stutters get shorter, pitch climbs. Every doubling makes the release feel bigger.
In our words: a short breath of silence just before the drop makes the return of the beat hit harder than any extra loudness could.
In our words: a single recorded voice can be stacked into a crowd by layering copies that are a few cents apart in tuning, a few milliseconds apart in time and spread across the stereo field.
In our words: a chopped voice memo can carry the whole hook: short slices of one phrase, tuned to the chord, repeat until they feel like a melody.
manifesto.system: A 16th-note clock runs three states: groove, build and drop, with a short gap between build and drop. While you hold, tension rises from 0 to 1 over the set number of bars. Tension thins out the kick, speeds the snare roll (every beat, every 8th, every 16th, then doubled), sweeps a high-pass filter up, adds a rising saw riser and your riser slot fitted to the build length, and re-triggers one chop of the voice memo in 2, 4 or 8 slices per beat. When you let go the build runs to the bar line, then the master is cut for the chosen number of beats and the drop begins at full level with a sidechain pump. The crowd stack plays several copies of the voice slot with random detune, timing and pan; chord voicing decides whether each copy sings the note, or a chord tone above it.

title: Long Exposure
kicker: GENERATIVE SYSTEMS · THE STUDIO AS A COMPOSITIONAL TOOL: STRETCH A MOMENT UNTIL IT BECOMES A PLACE
idea: A long photographic exposure turns a moving scene into one soft, still picture. This instrument does the same to your sounds. Three clouds of tiny grains, each cut from a different sample of yours, hover around chosen spots in the sound. The longer the exposure, the longer, denser and softer the grains, until a half-second of a voice becomes a standing wave of light. Slowly the clouds drift, the harmony changes by itself, and each cloud breathes in and out on its own long cycle, so the piece rewards both close listening and happily ignoring it. Capture any moment as a frame on the contact sheet and let the piece wander back through them.
controls: 6 slots (three granular clouds, bell, room tone that loops, pad); exposure (grain length, density and softness), scan speed, shutter freeze, position blur, stereo width, brightness and breathing for each cloud; key, six scales, six chord stacks and harmony drift time; twelve frames on a contact sheet (capture, recall, clear), automatic advance with walk, forward or random order; drag any lane to move a cloud; levels for every part; a bokeh view for the big screen.
how: Press PLAY and leave it. The three lanes show your samples with the part each cloud is reading, and grains appear as specks of light. Drag across a lane to move that cloud (keys 1 to 3 choose which); raise EXPOSURE to smear the sound into a texture. Click a frame on the contact sheet to recall it, or an empty one to capture the current moment. Press S for the shutter (freeze), A to let the frames advance by themselves, and F for the full-screen bokeh view. Load your own sounds with D and trim each with the S and E handles to choose the stretch of sound the cloud may read.

Load three very different recordings (a kitchen, a street and a piano note) into clouds 1 to 3. Capture four frames by dragging each lane to different places, then turn ADVANCE on at 20 seconds and walk away for ten minutes.

Put one long field recording in all three slots, trim each to a different third, and set BREATHING high. Listen for a while, then stop looking at the screen: notice which cloud you only notice when it fades away.

manifesto.name: Generative systems: the long exposure, stretching a moment into a place
manifesto.author: Inspired by tape-splicing, tape-loop and granular studio practice, and by generative music since the 1970s
manifesto.year: 1940s to now (granular sound theory 1947; tape splicing in the 1950s; digital granular synthesis from the 1980s)

ideas: In our words: a grain is a very short slice of sound, from a few hundredths to a few tenths of a second. Many grains laid close together fuse into a smooth sound that no longer sounds like a series of slices.
In our words: moving the reading position slowly through a recording stretches time without changing pitch, while holding it still freezes the sound like a held breath.
In our words: a studio can be treated as a compositional tool, not just a place to record. You set a system going, then shape it by listening, rather than writing every note.
In our words: ambient music can reward listening and ignoring at once. It should be interesting when you attend to it and unobtrusive when you do not.
In our words: letting several slow cycles of different lengths run together means the combined pattern takes a very long time to repeat, so the piece feels alive without being random.

title: Talea and Color
kicker: MUSIC THEORY · ISORHYTHM: A RHYTHM AND A PITCH LIST THAT NEVER LINE UP
idea: In the fourteenth century composers began building music from two repeating patterns of different lengths: a rhythm, called the talea, and a list of pitches, called the color. If the rhythm is twelve steps long and the pitch list seven notes long, each note meets each rhythm position in a new combination, and the music takes a long time to come back to where it started. This instrument gives you four voices, each with its own talea and color you can edit, change in speed (a voice at double speed is a diminution, at half speed an augmentation) and hear drift against the others. A tick marks every restart of the rhythm and a bell every restart of the pitches, so you can hear them part and meet again.
controls: 4 voices, each with a talea of 2 to 16 steps (click cells to toggle) and a colour of 2 to 12 scale degrees (click cells to step up or down), speed (x1, x2, x0.5 or x1.5) and octave; 2 marker sounds (talea restart and colour restart); rotate, new random talea or colour, reverse colour, align all voices; key, six scales, tempo, note length, reverb; the printout shows each voice's full cycle length in steps and bars and the time for all voices to realign; mute any voice; levels for every part; a green-bar paper VJ view that scrolls.
how: Press PLAY. Four voices play at once, each reading its own rhythm row (X is a note, a dot is a rest) and its own pitch row. The highlighted cell is the one just played. Click the cells to change them; click a voice's label (or press 1 to 4) to choose it, then press T to rotate its rhythm, X for a new rhythm, C for new pitches, V to reverse them and M to mute it. Change the lengths in the panel and watch the REPEATS AFTER figure grow. A restarts all voices together. Load a sound with D and trim it with the S and E handles to one clean note; the tool tunes it to every pitch.
