manifesto.name: Isorhythm: talea and color
manifesto.author: Composers of the fourteenth-century Ars nova in France and Italy, and later composers
manifesto.where: Western Europe; later taken up in many twentieth-century works
ideas: In our words: the talea is a rhythm pattern that repeats; the color is a list of pitches that repeats. The two are chosen to be different lengths.
In our words: when the lengths differ, each pitch lands on each part of the rhythm in turn, so the same ingredients keep producing new combinations.

In our words: the full cycle is the talea length times the colour length, divided by the greatest common divisor of the colour length and the number of notes in the talea, so small changes in length make large changes in how long the music takes to repeat.
In our words: the same melody can be played faster (diminution) or slower (augmentation) while other voices carry on at the original speed.
In our words: composers hid this structure inside the music for the ear to feel more than to count, and it was revived in the twentieth century as an early example of building music from a system.
manifesto.system: Each voice has a talea (a list of 1s and 0s, up to 16 long, of which the first T are used) and a color (a list of up to 12 scale degrees, of which the first C are used). A voice steps through its talea at its own speed. At each 1 it plays the next degree of its color, then moves on. Note length runs until the next 1 in the talea. Voice I (or the voice you choose) also fires a tick when its talea restarts and a bell when its colour restarts. The printout counts the notes (k) in the talea and shows the voice's cycle as T multiplied by C divided by the greatest common divisor of C and k, in steps and in bars at its speed, and the whole piece's realignment as the least common multiple of the voices' cycles.

title: Synchrony
kicker: NATURE · FIREFLIES, HEARTS AND CLAPPING CROWDS: HOW SEPARATE RHYTHMS FIND EACH OTHER
idea: In some forests, thousands of fireflies on riverbanks start the evening flashing at random and end it flashing in unison, with no leader. Load a kick or a soft thump into the Heartbeat slot and a long breath or drone into the Pad. Start with a negative coupling, then slowly raise it over a minute and let the music arrive: a track that builds itself out of disorder.

Put three different small sounds (a click, a vowel, a bell) in Glow A, B and C. Set QUANTISE on and the rate near 1.2 Hz, then change the key from the panel while the swarm plays, so the same rhythm reappears in a different harmony.

manifesto.name: Synchrony in nature
manifesto.author: Inspired by the study of coupled oscillators and of synchronous fireflies, cicadas and hearts
manifesto.year: 17th century to now (the first noted link between pendulum clocks in 1665; modern models from the 1970s)
manifesto.where: Riverbanks in South-East Asia and North America; laboratories; concert halls
ideas: In our words: a swarm can keep time with no leader, because each member adjusts to the others a little at a time.
In our words: a model of this treats each firefly as a clock that fires when it reaches the top and then starts again, nudged forward when it sees a flash.
In our words: if the nudge brings a clock closer to firing, the group slides into unison. If the nudge holds it back, the group spreads out.
In our words: the order meter measures how aligned the clocks are, from zero for scattered to one for perfect agreement.
In our words: audiences can fall into synchronised clapping in the same way, and hearts in the body keep time together by exchanging small signals.
manifesto.system: Each firefly has a phase from 0 to 1 that rises at its own natural rate (the flash rate varied by the spread) plus a little random noise. At 1 it flashes, plays a sound whose pitch is set by its horizontal position, and returns to 0. Every other firefly's phase is changed by the coupling multiplied by its own phase and by a weight that falls with distance (set by reach), so with a positive coupling those close to firing are pushed to fire, and with a negative one they are held back. A firefly pushed to 1 flashes at once. The order meter is the length of the average of all the phase vectors on a circle. When enough fireflies flash within 70 milliseconds, the heartbeat plays, and the pad level follows the order meter.
manifesto.dubious: Real firefly flashing is more complex than this simple pulse-coupled model; the tool is a teaching sketch of the general idea.

title: Simultaneous Discs
kicker: ART MANIFESTO · ORPHISM: COLOUR AS RHYTHM, AND THE WORLD AS EVERYTHING AT ONCE
idea: In the 1910s some painters in Paris dropped recognisable subjects and built pictures from discs and rings of pure colour, arguing that colour contrasts could carry the rhythm and movement that music has. They called the effect simultaneous contrast: a colour looks different depending on its neighbours, and a picture can seem to vibrate. This instrument turns that into a score. Six rings, each painted with up to twelve colours, turn at different speeds. Each time a coloured segment passes the reading line a note sounds, with the colour setting the pitch. Where neighbouring colours clash, notes ring louder.
controls: 6 slots (one per ring); 12 paintable colours, each a pitch class snapped to a chosen key and scale (seven scales); seconds per turn; per-ring segment count (3 to 12), speed ratio (from minus 3 to 3, negative turns backwards) and mute; simultaneity (one reading line to a fan, so the rings sound at different moments); contrast effect; note length; octave; reverb; random, close-hue and complementary painting; a bold VJ view where the whole screen takes the colour of the last note.
how: Press PLAY. The six rings turn and each segment that reaches the dark reading line sounds a note. Pick a colour from the palette and click or drag over the rings to paint them; alt-click a segment to pick its colour up. Press R, M or C to repaint everything randomly, in close hues or in complementary pairs. Raise SIMULTANEITY to fan the reading line out so the rings no longer sound together. Press 1 to 6 to mute rings and F for the full-screen view. Load your own sounds with D and trim each with its S and E handles; each ring plays its own sound.
try: Load a short sound (a pluck or a vowel) into all six slots, trim each S and E handle to a slightly different part of it, and paint all rings with the same colour. Then change a single segment to a distant colour and listen to how one note changes the whole texture.
Set SIMULTANEITY to zero so all six rings sound on one line, then raise it slowly to 100 percent. A tight chord first becomes a rolling pattern. Record that move as a WAV and use it as a transition.

Paint every ring in complementary pairs (press C), set the contrast effect to full and put a kick, a clap and a hat in rings 1 to 3. Rings with clashing neighbours will accent themselves, giving a rhythm you never programmed.

manifesto.name: Orphism: simultaneous contrast and colour rhythm
manifesto.author: Inspired by the Paris painters of the Orphist movement and the nineteenth-century colour theory they drew on
manifesto.where: Paris, with echoes in Germany and the United States
ideas: In our words: a picture can be built from pure colour and shape alone, with no recognisable subject.
In our words: placed side by side, two colours change each other's appearance, so a colour never looks the same in two places. This is called simultaneous contrast.
In our words: the painters compared colour contrasts to musical rhythm and harmony, and wanted a picture to move like a piece of music.
In our words: circles and discs were favoured because they suggest turning, and so time passing, in a still image.
In our words: they wanted to show the world as it is felt, with many things happening at once, instead of a single frozen view.
manifesto.system: Each ring has up to twelve segments, each painted one of twelve colours; a colour's number is a pitch class counted up from the key, which is snapped to the nearest note of the chosen scale. A ring turns at the base speed (one turn in the chosen number of seconds) multiplied by its ratio, and a negative ratio turns it backwards. When a new segment reaches the reading line, a note sounds on that ring's slot. The reading line is straight when simultaneity is zero, and each inner ring reads slightly further round as it rises. The loudness is scaled by how far the colour is around the colour circle from the segments of the neighbouring rings at that moment, mixed by the contrast setting.
manifesto.dubious: The Orphist group was small and its members disagreed about its aims; this tool presents only the broad ideas of colour contrast and rhythm, in our own words, and uses no image of any painting.

title: Stranger Duet
kicker: FOUND-SOUND PRODUCTION · TWO STRANGERS' RECORDINGS, ONE KEY, ONE TEMPO
idea: A lot of found-sound dance music starts with two recordings that have nothing to do with each other: a voice memo from a kitchen and a few words caught on a street. The producer's job is to introduce them. This instrument pitch-checks both recordings, nudges each into the key you choose, chops them into eight slices and lets them talk over a house or garage beat. In turn they take the floor, then reply in each other's gaps, then sing together a harmony apart. Drums, a field-recording bed and chord stabs sit underneath, and every pattern is a grid you can click.
controls: 7 slots (voice A, voice B, kick, clap, hat, field bed, chord stab); key, scale and tempo; MATCH TO KEY (pitch-detects A and B and sets each slot's pitch); two 16-step chop patterns of eight slices each (click to cycle, right-click to clear); turn length (1, 2 or 4 bars); interrupt chance; harmony interval; chop length; density; slice order (as drawn, walking, random, reversed); groove (house, garage, broken); swing; drum, bed, stab, reverb and voice levels; new letters, swap A and B; an airmail VJ view.
how: Press PLAY: voice A speaks, B answers, they trade and finally sing together, four turns in a cycle. Click a cell in the A or B row to choose which slice (1 to 8) plays on that step; right-click clears it. Press M to match both voices to your key, N for new random letters and X to swap the two voices' patterns. Open the deck (D), load a voice memo into slot 1 and a field recording into slot 2, and trim each with its S and E handles. Press F for the full-screen airmail view.
try: Put a voice memo in slot 1 and a street recording of someone else talking in slot 2, press M so both land in the key, then set the turn length to 1 bar. You get a conversation between two people who never met.
Choose the garage groove, set the harmony to +7 and the chop length to 3, then trim slot 1 to a single vowel with S and E. The vowel becomes a chord that follows the stabs.
Load a long field recording into slot 6, drop the drums to zero and turn the bed up. Record twenty bars with REC and use the result as the intro of a track.

manifesto.name: Found-sound production: the duet of two strangers
manifesto.author: Inspired by found-audio house and garage producers of the 2020s (no quotes, no copied patterns or audio)
manifesto.year: 2020s, from older sampling and call-and-response traditions
manifesto.where: Bedrooms, phones and dance floors
ideas: In our words: a phone recording of someone's voice carries emotion that no synth can fake, and most of that emotion survives being chopped small.
In our words: two found sounds only sound like a duet once they share a key and a pulse, so pitch-matching and tempo are the producer's matchmaking.
In our words: call and response is the oldest arrangement trick: one voice speaks, another answers in the gap, and then they join.
In our words: a field recording under the beat tells the listener where they are, which is why the room tone is not an afterthought.
In our words: a few chops repeated with small changes can build feeling faster than a long melody.
manifesto.system: Both voices are tested for their main pitch by autocorrelation (looking for the repeat length of the waveform). MATCH TO KEY finds the nearest note of your scale and writes the semitone shift into each slot's pitch. Each voice has a 16-step pattern whose cells hold a slice number from 1 to 8 (the trimmed region cut into eight). The arrangement cycles through four turns: A alone, B alone, trade (B only in A's gaps) and together (B sings A's slices a chosen interval above). Interrupt chance lets the quiet voice break in. The chord stabs follow a four-bar progression built from the scale you pick.
manifesto.dubious: No claim is made about any one producer's method; this is a general description of found-audio dance production, written in our own words.

title: Furniture Music
kicker: GENERATIVE SYSTEMS · MUSIC TO BE HEARD AND NOT LISTENED TO, UNLESS YOU WANT TO
idea: In the late 1910s a French composer imagined music that behaves like furniture: it fills a room, it is not the point of the evening, and nobody has to sit and face it. This instrument builds that idea as a generative system. Six loops of different lengths (primes, so they almost never line up) play your sounds, drifting through a scale. An ATTENTION dial slides between pure background and music that rewards close listening, when small bells, grace notes and hidden details appear. Oblique prompt cards, written in our own words, nudge the system when you are stuck.
controls: 6 slots (two pads, a bell, a voice, room tone, a hidden detail); six loop lengths from 5 to 97 seconds with a live readout of how long until they realign; attention (ignore to listen) with a slow automatic drift; wander (how often a loop changes note); note length; swell; speed (hurry the loops up to hear them combine); gifts (hidden details); key and scale; reverb and air; twelve prompt cards you can draw by hand or on a timer; per-loop mute; a wallpaper VJ view.
how: Press PLAY: the loops enter one by one and then keep returning at their own pace. Slide ATTENTION towards LISTEN to open the filters and let small details appear, or towards IGNORE to flatten them into the room. Press C for a prompt card (try the instruction on the system), 1 to 6 to mute a loop, and the up and down arrows for attention. Raise SPEED to hurry the loops so you can hear how six lengths combine. Open the deck (D), load your own sounds and trim each with S and E.
try: Put a single long chord from your sample library into slots 1 and 2, trim slot 2 with S and E to its quietest tail, and set the lengths to 31 and 37 seconds. Leave it running while you do something else, then slide ATTENTION to LISTEN to find out what was happening.

Load a voice memo of someone speaking into slot 4 and a field recording into slot 5. Set note length short, wander low and speed to 1. The voice returns every 29 seconds, always a little different, in a room that never quite repeats.
Set speed to 8 and lengths to 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23. Press REC for a minute and draw a card every few seconds; keep the take that surprises you and use it as a bed under a song.

manifesto.name: Furniture music: music that does not ask to be listened to
manifesto.author: Inspired by the furniture-music idea of a French composer in the 1910s, and by generative and ambient studio practice since the 1970s
manifesto.year: 1917 to 1920 (the idea); 1970s onwards (generative and ambient practice)
manifesto.where: Paris, then ambient studios and homes everywhere
ideas: In our words: music can be part of a room, like a chair or wallpaper, doing a quiet job rather than demanding that people stop and listen.
In our words: ambient music is best when it rewards you if you listen closely and costs you nothing if you do not.
In our words: loops of different lengths never line up the same way twice, so a very small amount of material can feel endlessly changing.
In our words: a good generative system is more like gardening than building: you set the conditions and let things grow.
In our words: a short written prompt can break a creative deadlock because it changes the question, not the answer.
manifesto.system: Six loops each have a length in seconds. When a loop comes round, it plays its slot's sound at a note chosen from your scale; with the wander setting it sometimes steps to a different degree first. ATTENTION opens each loop's filter and raises its level, and it controls how often hidden details (small bells, grace notes, a quiet high glint) appear. The slow drift moves attention up and down on its own so the music alternates between background and foreground. The loops realign after the least common multiple of their lengths, shown on screen. The prompt cards, written for this tool, make small changes to the system.
manifesto.dubious: The composer who coined the idea wrote little about how it should sound; this tool is our own reading of it, not a reconstruction, and quotes nothing.

title: Stochastic Rain
kicker: MUSIC THEORY · STOCHASTIC COMPOSITION: DRAW THE WEATHER, LET PROBABILITY PLAY THE DROPS
idea: In the 1950s some composers stopped writing every note and began writing the statistics of a sound mass: how dense it is, how high, how long each event lasts, how fast it changes. Chance, shaped by those figures, chooses the individual events. This instrument is a drawing board for that idea. Paint a density map of pitch against time, choose how onsets, lengths and glides are distributed, and probability scatters your sounds across it like rain on a window. Each loop is a different shower from the same weather, or the same shower if you fix the seed.
controls: 6 slots (four registers low to high, a short rain sound and a gliding voice); a 64 by 24 density map you paint and erase with adjustable brush; loop length 8 to 60 seconds; event rate; onset distribution (random, regular, clumped); event length mean and spread; glissando share and range; velocity spread; pitch quantised to a scale, chromatic or free; key, scale and range in octaves; seed with fix-and-repeat; live histograms of expected against actual events; shapes, clear, invert and blobs; a blueprint VJ view.
how: Press PLAY: a playhead sweeps the map and events fall wherever the paint is thick. Drag on the map to paint density and right-click or hold Alt to erase. Press G for another cloud, I to invert the map, C to clear, S for a new seed and X to fix the seed so every loop repeats exactly. Raise RATE for heavier rain, or switch onsets to REGULAR to hear the same map with the randomness taken out. Open the deck (D) to load your own sounds and trim each with S and E.
try: Load four sounds of rising brightness into slots 1 to 4 (a low pluck, a mid tone, a bell, a glassy hit) and paint one diagonal stripe from bottom left to top right. The shower climbs through your sounds as it climbs through the pitch map.
Fix the seed (X), paint a thin vertical stripe and set onsets to CLUMPED. Press REC for one loop and import it as a sample to chop: you have made a rhythm out of nothing but statistics.
Put a voice memo in slot 6 and set the glissando share to 80 percent with a range of 12 semitones. Paint only the top rows lightly: the voice glides in and out of the rain like a rumour.

manifesto.name: Stochastic music: composing with probability
manifesto.author: Inspired by composers who applied probability theory to music in the 1950s and 1960s, and by the mathematics of Poisson and Gauss
manifesto.where: Paris, with later work worldwide
ideas: In our words: a composer can describe a mass of sound by its statistics, such as density, register and speed of change, instead of writing each note.
In our words: the mathematics of chance, such as the Poisson law for random arrivals and the bell-shaped Gaussian curve, can choose individual events inside those limits.
In our words: a sliding pitch, a glissando, is a straight line on a pitch-time graph, so sound can be drawn as lines and areas as well as dots.
In our words: the law of large numbers means the more events there are, the closer the total sound matches the statistics, even though no single event can be predicted.
In our words: the composer's decisions move up a level, from choosing notes to choosing the rules that choose notes.
manifesto.system: The map is a grid of 64 time columns by 24 pitch rows holding a density from 0 to 1. For each column the expected number of events is the event rate times the column's length times the total density in that column. The actual number is drawn from the Poisson law (random onsets), or rounded (regular), or drawn and then pulled into clumps. Each event's row is chosen with probability proportional to the density in that column, its length from an exponential-style spread around the mean, its loudness from a spread, and a share of events glide. The pitch of each row is snapped to the scale, to the chromatic scale, or left free. With the seed fixed, every loop repeats; with it free, each loop is a new throw of the dice.
manifesto.dubious: Composers of the period worked in different ways and used computers and hand calculation; this tool shows only the general principle in our own words, and copies no score or data.

title: Wabi-Sabi Decay
kicker: NATURE AND PHILOSOPHY · WABI-SABI: BEAUTY IN THE IMPERFECT, IMPERMANENT AND INCOMPLETE
idea: Wabi-sabi is a Japanese way of seeing that finds beauty in things that are worn, weathered, modest and unfinished: a cracked bowl, a faded cloth, moss on a stone. This instrument plays a short piece that ages while you listen. Notes are forgotten one by one, the sound darkens like sun-faded cloth, the pitch wobbles like old tape, and a crackle of dust creeps in. You can mend the gaps with gold, the way a broken bowl is repaired with gold lacquer: the mend does not hide the damage but shows it, and the piece comes back changed.
controls: 6 slots (bowl, pluck, tap, breath, found voice, dust crackle); a generated 32-step, five-track piece with density and seed; life span from 8 to 200 bars with auto-age or a hand-drawn age slider; memory loss, darkening, pitch wobble, bit-crush and crackle amounts; MEND with gold (restores lost notes as brighter, changed notes); renew or hold at the end; key, scale, swing, reverb, level; a stencil-dyed cloth view and a big-screen VJ mode.
how: Press PLAY: a small sparse piece starts clean and begins to age. Watch the stencil cloth: each motif is a note, fading as it nears forgetting and showing a dotted ghost once it is gone. Press K (or MEND) to repair lost notes with gold, which come back an octave higher and a different note. Press N for a fresh piece, and drag the AGE slider by hand if you want to push time forwards or backwards. Open the deck (D) to load your own sounds and trim each with S and E.
try: Load a single recorded piano chord or guitar note into slots 1 and 2 and a handful of finger taps into slot 3. Set the life span to 30 bars and play it through: you will hear a tidy phrase turn into half-remembered fragments.

Drag AGE to about 70 percent and switch auto-age off. Mend three times with K and listen to which new golden notes appear. Press REC and keep the take: it is a damaged, repaired piece with its history audible.
Put a field recording in slot 4 and a voice memo in slot 5, set memory loss to maximum and crackle high, then let it renew itself. Each cycle leaves a different handful of survivors.

manifesto.name: Wabi-sabi: the beauty of the imperfect and impermanent
manifesto.author: Inspired by the Japanese aesthetic traditions of wabi-sabi and kintsugi (gold repair)
manifesto.year: Medieval origins; developed through the tea-house traditions of later centuries
manifesto.where: Japan
ideas: In our words: nothing lasts, nothing is finished and nothing is perfect, and noticing this can be a source of calm and beauty rather than sadness.
In our words: signs of age such as wear, cracks, fading and patina are part of an object's story and can make it more beautiful than when it was new.
In our words: kintsugi repairs a broken bowl with gold, so the break is celebrated as part of its history instead of hidden.
In our words: simplicity and restraint leave room for the listener or viewer to complete the picture themselves.
In our words: in sound, this suggests music that fades, wobbles and loses notes gracefully, and mends itself with something new.
manifesto.system: A 32-step, five-track piece is generated from your seed, density, key and scale. Every note is given a random point in the piece's life at which it will be forgotten; memory loss stretches or squeezes those points. As the age value rises from 0 to 1, notes that have passed their point go silent, notes close to it flicker, the filter closes, the pitch drifts slightly flat with random wobble, a bit-crushed copy of the sound fades in, and dust crackles become more frequent. MEND takes several forgotten notes, changes their pitch, lifts them an octave and makes them immune to forgetting for the rest of the piece, then turns the age back a little. At the end of its life the piece either holds or is renewed.
manifesto.dubious: Wabi-sabi is a broad and much-debated aesthetic, and the word is often used loosely; this tool is a small playful reading of the idea, not a statement of how it is practised.

title: Pattern and Decoration
kicker: ART MANIFESTO · PATTERN AND DECORATION: REPEAT, MIRROR, SPIN AND GLIDE A SMALL MOTIF INTO A WHOLE WALLPAPER OF MUSIC
idea: In the 1970s a group of artists argued that pattern, ornament and decoration deserved to be taken seriously as art, not dismissed as trim for the edges of important things. Pattern-makers have always used the same few moves: repeat a motif, mirror it, rotate it, or slide and flip it. Mathematicians found that these moves sort every repeating pattern into a small family of symmetry groups. Here you draw one bar-long motif, choose a symmetry group, and the wallpaper of music unrolls: each bar is the motif transformed, and three layers play it with different relationships, a little varied and a little ornamented, because exact repetition is only the start.
controls: 6 slots (layer 1 low and high, layer 2, layer 3, pulse tick, ornament voice); an 8 by 8 motif editor you paint; seven symmetry groups for the order of bars; independent relations for layers 2 and 3 (same, mirror, retrograde, spin, octave up, brick shift); stagger between layers; repeat-and-vary and ornament amounts; note length, swing, tempo, key, scale and octave; motif tools (random, clear, mutate, shapes); a banknote-engraving VJ view.
how: Press PLAY, then paint a few cells in the small motif grid on the left; the wallpaper on the right shows what each bar of each layer will play. Press G to change symmetry group and listen for the shape of the repeat: a hop is plain repetition, a mirror turns the tune upside down on alternate bars, a spin plays it backwards and upside down. Raise VARY to let the pattern wear and drift, and ORNAMENT to add small grace-note flourishes. Open the deck (D) to load your own sounds and trim each with S and E.
try: Load a short plucked note into slots 1 and 2, a marimba or wooden hit into slot 3 and a bell into slot 4. Draw a five-note zigzag, choose the full-symmetry group, and set layer 2 to mirror: you will hear the same tune answering itself upside down.
Choose the glide group, set stagger to 1 bar and VARY to 30 percent. Press REC for two minutes and keep the take: a patterned piece whose repeats never quite match.
Record yourself clapping a simple rhythm into slot 5 (the pulse) and tap the same rhythm as your motif. Then switch the group and hear that one rhythm become eight different grooves.

manifesto.name: Pattern and Decoration: ornament as art, and the symmetry of repeating patterns
manifesto.author: Inspired by the 1970s pattern-and-decoration art movement, and by the mathematics of symmetry groups used to classify repeating patterns
manifesto.year: 1970s (the movement); symmetry-group classification worked out in the 19th century
manifesto.where: Mainly the United States for the movement; pattern traditions worldwide
ideas: In our words: pattern and ornament have been undervalued as art, even though they are among the oldest and most widespread ways people make beautiful things.
In our words: a repeating pattern can only be built from a few moves: slide it along (translation), flip it (reflection), turn it (rotation), or slide and flip together (glide reflection).
In our words: in music these correspond to repeating a phrase, inverting it (turning it upside down in pitch), playing it backwards (retrograde), and both together.
In our words: strict repetition is soothing, and small variation or ornament keeps it alive, which is how traditional crafts often work.
In our words: ornament at the edges can become the main event if you give it your full attention.
manifesto.system: The motif is a grid of 8 steps by 8 pitch rows, one bar long. Each bar is made by applying a transformation to the motif: retrograde reverses the steps, inversion flips the pitch rows, a glide also shifts the steps sideways by half a bar, and a spin does retrograde and inversion together. The chosen group is a repeating list of those transformations, one per bar, for example a mirror group alternates the plain motif with its inversion. Layers 2 and 3 apply a further transformation on top, and the stagger moves them to different places in the list. Repeat-and-vary changes one note in a bar by a step with a given chance, and ornament plays a quick three-note flourish at the start of a bar.
manifesto.dubious: The pattern-and-decoration movement was varied and its members had different views; the group names here are friendly labels for transformations in music, not a claim about any artist's method, and no works are reproduced.
